A_target.statement:
Let $G$ be a [[Definition:Group|group]].
Let $G' = \sqbrk {G, G}$ be the [[Definition:Derived Subgroup|derived subgroup]] of $G$, and let $q: G \to G / G'$ be the [[Definition:Quotient Epimorphism|quotient epimorphism]].
Then $G / G'$ is [[Definition:Abelian Group|abelian]], and for every [[Definition:Group Homomorphism|homomorphism]] $\phi: G \to A$ into an [[Definition:Abelian Group|abelian group]] $A$ there exists a [[Definition:Unique|unique]] [[Definition:Group Homomorphism|homomorphism]] $\bar \phi: G / G' \to A$ such that:
:$\phi = \bar \phi \circ q$

B_source.statement:
Let $\phi: G \to H$ be a [[Definition:Group Homomorphism|group homomorphism]].
Then:
:$G / \map \ker \phi \cong \Img \phi$
where $\map \ker \phi$ is the [[Definition:Kernel of Group Homomorphism|kernel]] and $\Img \phi$ the [[Definition:Image of Mapping|image]] of $\phi$.

substitutions.the homomorphism f: an arbitrary homomorphism from G to an abelian group
substitutions.the kernel of f: a normal subgroup containing all commutators

derived.the universal property: factorization of every abelian-target homomorphism through G^{ab}

validity_conditions: the commutator subgroup must be normal in G, which holds since it is generated by a conjugation-stable set
the target must be abelian for commutators to lie in the kernel
minimality of [G,G] among such kernels is what gives universality, not just existence of the quotient
proof_plan:
From [[Derived Subgroup is Normal]], $G'$ is a [[Definition:Normal Subgroup|normal subgroup]] of $G$.
Hence the [[Definition:Quotient Group|quotient group]] $G / G'$ is defined.

For $x, y \in G$ we have:
:$\paren {x G'} \paren {y G'} \paren {x G'}^{-1} \paren {y G'}^{-1} = \paren {x y x^{-1} y^{-1} } G' = G'$
Thus $G / G'$ is [[Definition:Abelian Group|abelian]].

From the [[First Isomorphism Theorem for Groups]], $\phi$ factors through $G / \map \ker \phi$.
As $G' \subseteq \map \ker \phi$, the [[Definition:Mapping|mapping]] $\bar \phi: G / G' \to A$ given by:
:$\map {\bar \phi} {x G'} = \map \phi x$
is a [[Definition:Well-Defined Mapping|well-defined]] [[Definition:Group Homomorphism|homomorphism]] satisfying $\phi = \bar \phi \circ q$.
